newsitem.title: USA: Minn. gov. pitches Twins stadium funding in speech.
newsitem.headline: Minn. gov. pitches Twins stadium funding in speech.

text.p: Minnesota Gov. Arne Carlson used his state of the state address Thursday to make a pitch for public financing of a new stadium for the Minnesota Twins baseball team.
Calling sports "a part of Minnesota's community," Carlson told lawmakers that the state would lose the Twins if a new stadium is not supported.

He pointed out the state has stepped up financially to help other businesses such as Northwest Airlines and that the financing plan for the stadium "goes beyond subsidy" because it would give the state a ownership stake in the Twins.
"For a ten cent tax on cigarettes, we can own 49 percent of the Twins as well as a $350 million outdoor stadium. That is a good investment," Carlson said.
On Wednesday, lawmakers and the governor's chief negotiator on the stadium unveiled a plan to hike the state's cigarette tax by 10 cents a package to raise $34 million a year.

Proceeds from the tax hike, as well as revenues from a ticket tax at the new stadium would be used to finance the state's portion of the facility. One lawmaker said the revenues could be leveraged in a bond issue for the project.

Last week, the Twins owner said the team would contribute more than $157.5 million in construction and operating costs for the ballpark. Legislation for the financing plan is expected to be introduced by February.

Opposition to public financing for the stadium has already been voiced by House Minority Leader Steve Sviggum, R-Kenyon, who proposed Monday a bill to sell the Metrodome to its current tenants the Twins and the Minnesota Vikings football team for $1 and allow the teams to keep all revenue generated by the facility.
Carlson also reiterated his call for a $500 million tax cut fueled by a projected $1.4 billion budget surplus over the upcoming bienium.
In November, the governor proposed a one-time income tax rebate funded with one-third of the fiscal 1996-97 surplus projected at $522 million and $240 million in budget cuts.
Calling taxes on commercial and industrial property too high, Carlson said he asked state Revenue Commissioner Jim Girard to work with a bipartisan legislative group to address property tax reform.

The Republican governor also proposed the development of charter schools and tax credits for parents to hire math tudors, enroll students in foreign language classes, buy a home computer, attend a private school or home-school a child.

Carlson also said the state's budget will have a structural balance through 2002 and he noted that he met this week with Standard & Poor's Corp. in an attempt to raise the state's general obligation rating with that agency to triple-A. Minnesota is already rated triple-A by Moody's Investors Service and Fitch Investors Service.
